title: There is no unified self
subtitle: You have more than one self
author: Kenneth J Gergen
introduction: Throughout history the West has promoted the unified self. Whether it is the Christian emphasis on inner purity or the rationalist focus on eliminating contradictions in thought and reason, we have long believed that the unified self is a worthy objective. In this article, Kenneth Gergen argues that the desire for self-unity is ultimately mistaken. To adapt to the ever-changing modern world and to work with others to achieve the public good, we must shift our starting point from the fixed unified self to fluid and complex social processes.
body:
This article is presented in association with Closer To Truth.

Western culture has had long romance with the idea of a mind within the body, a regnant force somewhere behind the eyes. One could trace such dedication to Aristotle, and his complex vision of an animating soul. Christianity picked up the thread but anointed it with a spiritual oil. For Descartes and Kant the soul reappears in secularised form as thought process, while Freud later spied unconscious forces twisting and disturbing the thinker. One might say that that the realm behind the eyeballs is like a blank slate upon which culture may inscribe the fantasies of the times. How could it be otherwise? If we invent an imaginary space, what are the limits and evidential barriers in how we select its population?

This is not to argue for abandoning this tradition of speculation. To abandon all of humankind’s imaginaries would rob us of most that’s worth living for. These attributed ingredients of the psyche have served not only to unite communities and foster a nurturing sense of being, but also – precisely because of their undecidability – they sustain the vital questions of “who am I?” and “who are we together?” To terminate such questioning is to seal the door of imagination itself.

At the same time, attention to the fit between such assumptions and the conditions of the times is important. How does the embrace of a given belief function within existing conditions; how does it contribute to well-being; what is lost; who is oppressed?  And if such concepts as the sanctified soul or unconscious pariahs are losing their salience in contemporary life, what are their replacements, and what are their promises? In effect we shift from wobbly questions of ontological justification to pragmatic questions of the relationship between our beliefs about persons and the contribution of these beliefs to human wellbeing.

With deep roots in Western history, and blossoming in the 20th century, we find a widely shared belief in the ideal of what can be termed a unified self.

It is just here that I want to take up a particular vision of mental life – embedded within our common understandings and institutions – which now threatens the viability of cultural life.  With deep roots in Western history, and blossoming in the 20th century, we find a widely shared belief in the ideal of what can be termed a unified self. There are many species of this belief. Possibly drawing from the Christian tradition of the purified soul, along with Thomas Merton’s disquisition on the true self, there remains a strong belief in an interior core. Both in psychiatry and popular culture, that core is typically characterised by an absence of contradiction. Closely related is the cultural ideal of authenticity, the coherence between one’s true self and one’s public actions. Similarly, a common value is placed on integrity, remaining true to ones’ principles. Within the 20th century, the vision of unity takes a cognitive turn.  With philosophers such as Descartes and Kant creating a vision of reason as the central ingredient of mind, and logical positivism providing the guiding rationale for modernist science, rationality became a chief means of judging the quality of the individual mind. Promoted in our educational institutions, the coherent and well-ordered essay was a marker of superior thought.

The century’s sciences of mind – psychology and psychiatry – have offered unstinting support for the ideal of unity. For psychologist George Kelly the healthy mind strives for coherence; for Erik Erickson the state of identity (a unified sense of self) is an achieved stage of human development; for R.D. Lang the divided self is the source of schizophrenia; for Gregory Bateson and his colleagues, a child’s exposure to double binds (irreconcilable demands) leads to mental illness; while psychiatrists define pathology in terms of multiple personality and schizoid (or “split”) behaviours.  And in the culture at large we find best-selling books on embracing your inner truth, locating the confidence to be yourself, and on building, awakening, uncovering, and cultivating authenticity.

To be sure, these many variations on the vision of a unified self have served useful purposes over the centuries. Perhaps most important, they have provided both a meaningful goal toward which one should strive and a means of protecting the social order. Whether it is currying God’s favour, locating the lodestone of one’s being, or successfully reaching a stage of development, life has a valued direction.  At the same time, such pursuits also signify one’s identifiability in the social order. They inform one’s family, community, religion, or political party that one is reliably and fundamentally “this person” and no other. In deviating one confronts a ready-made array of epithets:  two-faced, con-artist, fake, slippery, untrustworthy; on the more serious side there is fraud, blasphemy, and treason. A unified self is essentially a community’s person of character.

But now to address the pragmatic question – namely, the personal and cultural utility of this multi-layered vision of a unified self. The 20th century is sometimes called the century of science, carrying with it the vast hope and promise of science for benefitting humankind and the world. That hope and promise were indeed fuelled by wide-ranging discoveries in physics, chemistry and biology, and an enormous array of innovative technologies that directly enhanced the quality of life. With the emergence of the social sciences, we could also anticipate knowledge for creating perfect lives, both individually and for society as a whole – conflict free, well ordered, efficient, and continuously improving.

Yet, as we have learned, the impact of science on cultural life is far from what was promised. Yes, there is a continuous process of ordering, with new laws, institutions, and technologies continuously striving to bring us into step. But every ordering is also a disordering. The electric light, automobile, radio, television, and high-speed computing devices among them, have radically altered the character of social life. And because every technological innovation breeds further innovation, we now confront the uncontrollable production of disordering devices.  Especially relevant in the present context are technologies of sociation, that is, technologies such as the radio, air travel and television in earlier times to current developments in cell phones and the internet – all of which increase the range, numbers, and availability of other people in our lives.

There is first the disconnect between a world in rapid and unpredictable change, and the individual’s embrace of an obdurate core.

It is in just this context that we begin to encounter the dysfunctionality inherent in the vision and desirability of the unified self. There is first the disconnect between a world in rapid and unpredictable change, and the individual’s embrace of an obdurate core. In a world in which survival depends increasingly on flexibility and creative adaptation, the strong character may soon become an anachronistic niche item. On the societal level, it is just this process that is splitting nations between the tech savvy and the true believers; on the global level it is Thomas Friedman’s Lexus and the olive tree. In terms of cultural evolution, we must also realise that regardless of the ideal of the unified self, the demands of cultural life are slowly rendering it obsolete. David Riesman realised the trend as early as the 1950s, decrying the loss of “inner direction,” as the modern organisation called one to be “other directed.” More recently, there are Zygmunt Bauman’s recurring critiques of the rootless liquidity of human relations, and psychologists’ increasing concern with self-alienation and the healing of fragmented selves.

We thus confront the challenge of the new imaginary. What may be envisioned as the next turn in the concept of the person?  There is despair in the vision of an empty self, wandering aimlessly and uncaringly into a meaningless future. How shall we fill the void, and with what consequences?  Possibly prophetic, are the words of the pioneer psychologist William James, “A man has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize him.”  While James was pleased to fill the mental slate with characters, this marginal comment shifted the focus from the internal world of the individual to the social milieu in which the individual resides. This shift is also reflected in the works of Vygotsky, Bakhtin, and Erving Goffman, where individual functioning becomes subservient to social process.

The essentialising and valorising of a unified core invite narcissism, instrumentalism, and competitiveness.

This is not a trivial turn as it is precisely the social world that has traditionally functioned as the enemy to the unified self. The demands, expectations and seductions of others represent corrosive forces to be overcome in the valiant quest for self-unity. At the same time, it is a turn that has been increasingly buttressed by critics of individualist ideology. The essentialising and valorising of a unified core invite narcissism, instrumentalism, and competitiveness. Simultaneously undermined are attempts to achieve public goods such as environmental sustainability and world peace. In a world of autonomous individuals, “public good” is an inconvenient abstraction.

It is in this context that we increasingly find attempts to articulate a more relationally centred alternative to the unified self. Charles Taylor’s work has been pivotal in this respect. With a keen appreciation for the social matrix from which we emerge as persons, he searches for a revision in our understanding of individual authenticity. In a related vein, Martha Nussbaum’s cosmopolitanism is vitally concerned with relational conditions in the world but simultaneously pays respect to individual autonomy.

More radically, let us suppose that this process is the origin for anything we would call an individual self. The process precedes the person, just as the dance precedes the dancers.

As I have come to see it, to become free from the debilitating grip of the unified self we must shift our starting point from the individual to social process. More radically, let us suppose that this process is the origin for anything we would call an individual self.  The process precedes the person, just as the dance precedes the dancers.  As the process shifts its character, so do the attributes of the participants. The individual body, as it might be called, is akin to a Heideggerian standing reserve, a mobile mass of potentials to “be somebody” as the flow of relations plays on. Concern shifts, then, from care of the person, or care of the other, to care for the relational process. From what forms of relationship do we flourish? Here again is a pragmatic question for conversations now in progress.
